Paired harm built on a 3-sample no-memory majority is noisy, since Recuris saw 25.9% breakage from re-running identical tasks. If harm cannot be predicted from cheap features, the gate collapses to 'never use memory'. The write-gate half overlaps heavily with Janus, Recuris and InfoMem.

ranking.title: What Do Streaming 3D Models Remember? Continual-Learning Accuracy Matrices, Scene-Change Plasticity Tests, and a Delta-Rule Reset Law
ranking.rationale: The read-only per-frame probes, the A-B-A tests and the 3RScan ghost-rate and latency tests are cheap and hard to scoop, and a released benchmark would be cited. It brings the CL accuracy-matrix vocabulary into 3D, it reuses the same hooks as plans 1 and 4, and the 8 GPU-hour pilot includes a sanity gate on the prior control.
ranking.biggest_weakness: Being a benchmark, its impact depends on adoption. Predicting the best reset period with a linear delta-rule model of a nonlinear transformer state (Spearman >= 0.6 over 20 or more sequences) is a stretch, write-protect-on-revisit is close to TTSA3R/ReCal3R, and the probes only fully work for the CUT3R family.

ranking.title: Do Sequential Knowledge Editors Collapse in Writes or in Live Facts? Superseded-Key Protection and Garbage Collection in Null-Space Editors
ranking.rationale: It gives a sharp, falsifiable mechanism: relation-independent subject keys pile up in AlphaEdit's cache_c and attenuate each revision harmonically. That can be checked with a CPU simulation in 2 days and a 10 GPU-hour GPT2-XL run on real AToKe-ME chains. The 2x2 rollback x downdate factorial and the live-facts vs writes scaling law give it a diagnostic core, and it maps the doc's 'what to keep or evict' question onto the weight store.
ranking.biggest_weakness: The novelty check ran no searches at all, and the fix is a one-line rank-1 downdate. The z-optimisation margin across 5 layers may absorb the attenuation, so binary efficacy barely moves, and the result only applies to editors in the AlphaEdit/MEMIT_seq/NSE family.

ranking.title: Depth, Not Time: Lineage Depth Predicts When Rewritten Agent Memory Rots, and Depth-Bounded Regeneration Prevents It
ranking.rationale: It offers a quantitative explanation of the doc's improve-plateau-decline result. Holding experience fixed while varying the schedule is a clean test that the competing models (2609.25052, Yang et al.) cannot pass. The Hidden-Rule World with exact per-insight scoring runs on CPU and gives fast signal, and depth-bounded regeneration and tree consolidation are cheap practical fixes.
ranking.biggest_weakness: Predicting t* within 25% of stream length on ALFWorld and ARC, pre-registered from HRW parameters, is very ambitious. Two channel parameters are probably too crude, ARC with an 8B consolidator may sit at the floor, and the result could shrink to 'don't rewrite in place', which 2605.12978 already says.

ranking.title: Frequency Is Not a Timescale: When Do Multi-Frequency (CMS) Memories Actually Consolidate?
ranking.rationale: This is the cheapest plan of the 13. The pilot already exists and confirms the lemma to machine precision. It tests the doc's 'main bet' (Nested Learning/HOPE CMS) with a falsifiable claim, and MQAR on DeltaNet with slow MLP levels runs in under 10 GPU-hours. A closed-form downscaling and C_k design rule would be useful.
ranking.biggest_weakness: Once stated, the lemma is obvious (Hinton and Plaut 1987, Smith et al. 2006). Real HOPE chains its levels and uses per-level momentum or other optimizers, which probably breaks the degeneracy (kill criterion 2), and novelty was checked without a live search.

ranking.title: Folding Sessions into Weights: When Can Linear-Attention Fast States Be Consolidated in Closed Form?
ranking.rationale: It takes on the doc's open problem directly: consolidating fast state into slow parameters without gradients and without storing text, measured on the recall-vs-KL frontier the doc cares about. Consolidation is a d x d solve, the models are 1.3-1.5B, and the injection sanity check gives a decisive answer within days.
ranking.biggest_weakness: Queries in a fresh context will likely not line up with the keys written during the session, and facts in small recurrent LMs may live in MLPs, so recovering 50% of recall at KL < 0.02 looks optimistic. Gradient state-tuning may dominate the frontier. Novelty is unverified (Chen et al. 2024, FAAST, 'LMs Need Sleep'), and the fla-hub checkpoint names come from memory.

ranking.title: Rent, Buy, or Let It Expire: Competitive Consolidation of Changing Facts from a Retrieval Store into a Small LM
ranking.rationale: It is a formal and original take on the doc's central question of what moves to the weights and when. Rent-or-buy with purchases that expire and rent that depends on store size is new, and the synthetic world plus theory runs on CPU.
ranking.biggest_weakness: It has too many parts: a Wikidata revision crawl, pageview demand, MEMIT/AlphaEdit covariance re-derivation for Qwen 0.5B/1.5B, a Pythia checkpoint difference-in-differences study, and a coupled ILP. Edits to models of 1.5B or smaller often fail to generalise to paraphrases, so the likely answer is 'never buy'. ALLOT's method section is still unread, and the N-coupling breaks the clean 2-competitive bound.

ranking.title: Revisits Break Persistence of Importance: An Oracle-Audited, Revisit-Stratified Study of KV-Cache Eviction in Streaming 3D Transformers
ranking.rationale: The future-attention oracle and the revisit-stratified AUROC test of RegVGGT's persistence assumption are new to 3D, and the released revisit labels would help plans 1, 2 and 4 as well.
ranking.biggest_weakness: The fix is already covered by RetrieveVGGT, STAC and OVGGT, and the field has about 10 bounded-cache papers. Logging per-layer attention for 500-frame clips needs an 80 GB card and 1-2 TB of disk, and closed-loop oracle iterations multiply the cost. Long-gap revisits are rare in clips of 500 frames or fewer, which invites a selection-bias critique.

ranking.title: Overwrite or Wait? Quickest-Change-Detection Belief Slots and an Entrenchment Law for LLM Agent Memory
ranking.rationale: Framing the overwrite decision as Bayesian change detection with stance-dependent noise is principled, and week 1 runs on CPU. Temporary-scope sub-states with expiry and calibrated slot posteriors are real differences from prior work.
ranking.biggest_weakness: The space is crowded (BeliefMem, BBT, MemTxn, MemOps, MINTEval, CMI), and the slot schema covers only attribute-like facts. Extraction errors from a 7B model on hedges and scope may outweigh any gain from the gating rule. For a linear filter, the 'entrenchment law' amounts to saying latency grows linearly in repetitions, so it says little.

ranking.title: Evict the Text, Keep the Address: Self-Test-Gated Eviction Turns a Retrieval Store into an Index over a Small LM's Weights
ranking.rationale: It asks a good, under-asked question about consolidation: when can the store forget? The shuffled-code, format-prime and base-model controls are well designed, and the pilot on Qwen2.5-0.5B is cheap.
ranking.biggest_weakness: The novelty check ran no searches, and the premise paper (2607.11020) is unverified. Recovery from a cue may just be generic task-alignment priming (Spurious Forgetting). It needs repeated full fine-tuning across 20 episodes and several address types, and LLMLingua-2 or plain replay may dominate it on the Pareto curve.

ranking.title: How Much Replay Does a Pretrained ViT Need, and When? Replay-demand laws and a KL thermostat
ranking.rationale: It applies lessons 1 and 2 to classic vision CL, with Mammoth tooling ready and clear r*(T) and proxy-race measurements. The split of drift into recency leak and within-old-class drift is a nice touch.
ranking.biggest_weakness: This is crowded classic CL ground: Prabhu et al. found that uniform ER is hard to beat at equal compute, and LoRA-adapted pretrained ViTs barely forget, so r* may be close to 0. Only 50 or fewer tasks cannot tell log growth from sqrt growth. The novelty check could not run, so FOREVER and MSSR are unread, and the plan does little for the doc's frontier problems.

judge.start_here:
Start with a shared two-week CUT3R/TTT3R hook sprint, about 25-30 GPU-hours on one 24-48 GB card. Run the oracle-retrieval test from plan 1 (Keep the State) and the replay pilot from plan 4 (Rewrite or Advance) on the same 7-Scenes, TUM and ScanNet sequences. Both need the same three hooks: a state dump to CPU, a read-only decode (update=False), and an extra view injected into the view list with update masks. Together the two tests decide whether the recurrent state is memory worth keeping, refreshing or restoring, or only a cache of its frames. Whichever result is positive becomes the main paper, and the probes from plan 2 come almost free from the same runs, giving the benchmark or analysis chapter. This fits the user's 3D interest, needs no training, and gets a go/kill answer within 2 weeks.

As a cheap hedge outside 3D, spend 2 CPU days on the linear simulation from plan 10 (AlphaEdit garbage collection), then about 10 GPU-hours on GPT2-XL with AToKe-ME chains. First run the live novelty search that plan's check never managed, and read 2606.26783.

If the user prefers LLM agent memory over 3D, start with plan 6 (Do-No-Harm). Its paired logs allow offline gate replay, so one round of stream runs answers both the harm question and the gate question.
synergies: Thesis chapter 'Is the recurrent 3D state a memory?' (plans 1, 2, 4). Plan 2 measures what the state retains (accuracy matrices, half-life), plan 4 refreshes it with replay under a fixed pass budget, and plan 1 banks, restores and transfers it across sessions. All three use the same CUT3R/TTT3R checkpoint, the same hooks (snapshot dump, read-only decode, view injection) and the same datasets (7-Scenes, TUM, ScanNet, NRGBD).

The revisit labeller from plan 3 (novel / short-gap / long-gap frames from GT frustum overlap) and its released loop and A-B-A splits can serve as the shared evaluation for plans 1, 2 and 4. Plan 2's KV-cache arm (StreamVGGT/STream3R) can reuse plan 3's eviction interface, giving one paper that covers recurrent, KV and pointer memory side by side.

Chapter 'Safe consolidation of text memory' (plans 6 and 7). They share the Dynamic Cheatsheet/ACE builders, Qwen3-8B on vLLM, and the Game of 24 / ARC / MATH streams. Plan 7 explains why consolidated memory rots (lineage depth), and plan 6 bounds the damage (paired conformal gate). Plan 6's paired logs can also supply the regression labels plan 7 needs.

Chapter 'Consolidating into the weight store and garbage-collecting it' (plans 5, 9, 10). They share CounterFact, zsRE, WikiFactDiff and AToKe, Qwen2.5-0.5/1.5B and GPT2-XL, and EasyEdit with covariance stats. Plan 10's write ledger and exact downdate can be the 'buy' operation in plan 5, so that expired purchases are properly evicted. Plan 9 answers when the store copy can be dropped after a buy.

Plans 5 and 8 both need per-relation change hazards fitted from Wikidata revision history. One crawl can serve both: plan 8's hazards set its change-point priors, and plan 5's hazards make purchases expire.

Fast-state theory (plans 11, 13, and the delta-rule theory in plan 2). All use flash-linear-attention and delta-rule algebra. Plan 13's shared-loss fast/slow analysis says when plan 11's closed-form fold can keep content, and the same retention/hazard maths gives plan 2 its reset-period law for TTT3R. Plan 13 itself names TTT3R plus a slow level as a stretch goal, which links the theory to the 3D chapter.

Plans 12 and 6 both measure drift relative to a reference: sentinel KL against write-time logits in one, paired harm relative to no memory in the other. Both rest on RL's Razor reasoning and could share an analysis section on which drift sensors predict forgetting.
missing_angles: Consolidating 3D state into weights. All five 3D plans are training-free and keep memory in the state, the KV cache or an external bank. None moves a revisited scene into a tiny per-scene adapter (for example rank-4 LoRA on CUT3R's decoder or pose head, trained for a few seconds) or decides when a scene has earned one. This is the doc's open consolidation problem in its own 3D setting, and it fits in a few GPU-hours.

Deletion and unlearning across all four stores. When a user or privacy request removes an item, it has to leave the buffer, the edited weights, the fast state and the retrieval index together. A small study on 1.5B-or-smaller LMs, or on CUT3R scenes, of residual leakage after deleting from one store only fits the doc's privacy failure mode and needs little compute.

Management on the retrieval side of the external store. 2604.27003 says the bottleneck moves to memory access, but no plan manages the index itself: interference-aware dedup and merging, deciding how many entries get context slots, or rebalancing by retrieval competition among near-duplicate keys. Retrieval error e(N) appears only as a cost term in plan 5.

Picking the store from the type of change (Harrington et al. 2607.07847). A cheap meta-router that classifies an incoming change (new fact, revision, new skill, distribution shift) and sends it to context, store, adapter or nothing, evaluated on existing sequential protocols with API models, is absent. Plans 5 and 8 cover only facts.

Slot management in memory layers. Sparse memory finetuning (2510.15103) is the doc's clearest weight-store success, yet no plan studies which slots to allocate, reuse or evict in a small memory-layer model, or how slot occupancy grows over a stream. Feasibility depends on whether public small memory-layer checkpoints exist.

Online RL as the consolidation path under noisy rewards. The doc says online RL handled knowledge updates best but broke under noisy rewards. A small study of reward-noise-gated consolidation, for example GRPO on 0.5B Qwen with a KL budget, is missing.

Memory management for embodied or 3D-language agents, for example object-goal navigation or 3D question answering with an episodic 3D memory that must be pruned or merged. It would connect the 3D and agent tracks and can run on simulators with small models.

Cross-cutting compute accounting. None of the plans reports results in a common unit such as memory-operation FLOPs per retained item across stores, which the doc's lesson 1 suggests and which would let the portfolio's chapters be compared directly.
overclaim_flags: Plan 5 (Rent, Buy, or Let It Expire): 160 GPU-hours has to cover MEMIT/AlphaEdit plus LoRA on 2 models x 1k facts, the Pythia checkpoint study, nine 24-month policy streams and re-derived covariances for Qwen 0.5B/1.5B, all after a heavy Wikidata history crawl. The 'within 2x of clairvoyant' claim does not follow from classic ski-rental once purchases expire and rents are coupled through N. Edits to small models may not generalise to paraphrases at all.

Plan 3 (KV eviction audit): 140 GPU-hours and 1-2 TB of disk understate the cost of fp16 attention logging over 24 layers x ~1041 tokens x 500 frames, plus closed-loop oracle iterations re-run on an 80 GB card. The oracle is described as a reference, but the hypothesis still depends on it recovering 50% or more of the loss.

Plan 7 (Depth, Not Time): pre-registered prediction of the accuracy peak t* within 25% of stream length on ALFWorld and ARC, from two parameters measured in a synthetic world, is very optimistic. ALFWorld (10 policies x 3 seeds x 2 consolidators) in about 60 GPU-hours and an ARC stream with Qwen3-8B (likely at the floor) are both tight.

Plan 6 (Do-No-Harm): it relies on 'claude-haiku-5-5 at an unverified per-token price'; check the model name and price before budgeting. Three no-memory samples per item across 4 datasets x 3 builders x 3 seeds, plus thinking-mode ablations, may exceed 160 GPU-hours. Under memory drift the offline CRC guarantee does not hold strictly, and ACI gives only a long-run average.

Plan 2 (What Do Streaming 3D Models Remember): predicting the best reset period with Spearman >= 0.6 from a linear delta-rule model of a nonlinear transformer state is an overreach. The R^2 gap >= 0.2 for displacement vs elapsed frames is asserted, not motivated. 3RScan's low-resolution Tango imagery may break CUT3R.

Plan 11 (Folding Sessions): recovering 50% or more of in-context recall at generic KL < 0.02 with a closed-form fold on 1.3B fla-hub models (weak in-context recall, keys misaligned in a fresh context) is optimistic. The checkpoint names and the Chen et al. arXiv ID are unverified.

Plan 1 (Keep the State): a gain of 10 or more points in relocalisation recall without Sim(3) alignment, and 20% or more ATE reduction against Scal3R, are confident targets given Anchor3R's frame-dependence finding. RIO10 is available only on request, which may leave just about 10 usable pairs for the headline change test.

Plan 4 (Rewrite or Advance): 15% or more median ATE gain over an oracle-tuned stride, including on exploration sequences and stacked on ReCal3R/TTSA3R, is a high bar after AFG's 51% gains from gating alone.

The 'partially_novel' verdicts for plans 9, 10, 11, 12 and 13 came from novelty checks that ran no live searches (budget exhausted, arXiv DNS failures). Treat them as unverified, not as evidence of novelty. Plans 1-8 also rest only on search snippets, with no paper opened except MemOps.

Plan 13 (Frequency Is Not a Timescale): 130 GPU-hours overstates the need, since most of the work runs on CPU. The overclaim is in framing: the lemma holds only for parallel levels under plain SGD on a shared loss, so presenting it as a finding about HOPE/CMS needs the nonlinear audit to come out positive.

Plan 8 (Overwrite or Wait): the 'entrenchment law' for a linear coupled fast/slow filter (latency roughly linear in R) is close to a definition. Calling it a law of multi-timescale memory overstates it.
